documents.abstract: This article examines the specific features of developing health-promoting competence among students in the context of modern digital pedagogical technologies aimed at increasing students' physical and health-promoting activity during academic classes and outside teaching hours; it describes the pedagogical conditions for the use of digital technologies in physical and health-promoting activities; and sets out methodological recommendations for applying these technologies in the educational process to improve physical mobility and foster a responsible attitude amongst students towards maintaining and strengthening their own health. The aim of the article is to provide a theoretical justification for the specific features of developing health-preserving competence within the student community through physical education in the context of the digitalisation of education. The novelty lies in the systematisation of digital tools for developing health-preserving competence among students, the analysis of their didactic potential, as well as in clarifying the role of digital technologies and the integration of traditional physical education methods with digital educational tools. The research is based on the comprehensive use of methods such as the systems-analytical method, content analysis, comparative analysis and descriptive statistics, and the method of structural generalisation. The authors of the article concluded that digital resources are capable of ensuring access to physical education and health information, supporting the personalisation of physical exercise, monitoring physical activity and promoting the development of self-control skills, however, their pedagogical value is determined not by the technology itself, but by their ability to foster in students a lasting intrinsic motivation for a healthy lifestyle and a willingness to organise health-promoting activities independently. The digital educational environment should be viewed as an additional pedagogical resource, not as an end in itself or as a modernisation of physical education tools, but as a means of transitioning to a more student-centred model of health promotion.

Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs)-synthesized data to enable representation learning for cold-start entities has emerged as a promising solution for addressing cold-start recommendations. However, existing studies often over-rely on LLM-generated data while neglecting the detrimental noise it may introduce. This work investigates data filtering mechanisms to remove detrimental synthetic samples. One promising approach is to use influence functions to measure the influence of each data. Nevertheless, a technical challenge arises because accurate influence estimation requires an unbiased reference model, which cannot be satisfied due to the existence of unknown noise. To address this, we conduct a theoretical analysis, revealing that when the goal is to identify a small subset of highly harmful data, even a biased model can still reliably capture the most detrimental points. Building on this insight, we propose a Progressive Influence Function-based method (PIF) for data filtering. PIF iteratively refines influence estimates: it repeatedly trains a new reference model after removing the previous step's most harmful data and reassesses influence. As detrimental data is progressively removed, the reference model becomes less biased. Finally, PIF ensembles influence estimates across iterations for robust filtering. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of our approach.

Model-attribution classifiers can often identify which language model produced a text, making model-specific writing patterns a signal of provenance. Accurate attribution on unmodified text, however, does not show whether the prediction still identifies the original source after deliberate rewriting. We formulate this problem as targeted fingerprint transfer: rewriting one model's output so that attribution classifiers assign it to a chosen target model. We study summarization, where different models receive the same document and express the same underlying content, providing a controlled setting for conditional generation. We introduce ForgePrint, a search-then-distil framework that first searches for rewrites that move attribution toward a target fingerprint, then distils the selected rewrites into a one-pass 4B Student model. On CNN/DM, the Student reaches 70.2% target success rate, outperforming both its Teacher (54.1%) and the strongest of six published rewriting baselines (39.3%), against held-out classifiers that are never queried by the attack. It also reaches 68.3% target success when transferring summaries from an open model toward chosen commercial models. These results show that fingerprint detectability should not be conflated with source authenticity, and that text-only attribution can provide misleading evidence of model identity under targeted rewriting, even when it is accurate on unmodified text.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technological innovations of the twenty-first century, fundamentally changing the way individuals learn, work, communicate, and solve complex problems. Although AI has become a prominent component of modern society only in recent decades, its conceptual foundations extend back several centuries through philosophical discussions concerning human intelligence, logical reasoning, and mechanical computation. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence represents a multidisciplinary journey involving computer science, mathematics, cognitive psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, engineering, statistics, and data science. Continuous advancements in computational power, algorithmic development, data availability, and digital infrastructure have enabled AI to evolve from theoretical concepts into intelligent systems capable of performing tasks that traditionally required human intelligence. The earliest ideas related to artificial intelligence originated long before the invention of computers. Ancient civilizations imagined intelligent machines capable of mimicking human behaviour through myths, literature, and mechanical inventions. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, philosophers and mathematicians such as René Descartes, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and George Boole contributed foundational concepts related to logic, reasoning, symbolic representation, and mathematical computation. Their work laid the intellectual groundwork for the development of computational systems capable of representing knowledge and making logical decisions.The modern evolution of Artificial Intelligence began during the twentieth century with the rapid advancement of computing technologies. In the 1930s and 1940s, significant progress in mathematical logic and computer science established the theoretical basis for intelligent machines. Alan Turing introduced the concept of a universal computing machine and later proposed the famous Turing Test, which examined whether a machine could demonstrate behaviour indistinguishable from that of a human being. Turing's pioneering contributions remain fundamental to contemporary AI research because they established that machines could potentially perform intelligent reasoning through computational processes. A major milestone occurred in 1956 during the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester. This conference formally introduced the term "Artificial Intelligence" and established AI as an independent scientific discipline. Researchers believed that human intelligence could be represented computationally and that machines could eventually perform reasoning, learning, language understanding, and problem-solving. The Dartmouth Conference inspired widespread academic interest and initiated decades of intensive research into intelligent computing systems.The period between the late 1950s and early 1970s is often referred to as the early development phase of Artificial Intelligence. During this era, researchers developed symbolic AI methods that emphasized logical reasoning, rule-based systems, theorem proving, and problem-solving algorithms. Early AI programmes successfully solved mathematical problems, played strategic games such as chess, and demonstrated limited natural language capabilities. Optimism surrounding AI research increased substantially as scientists believed that general human-level intelligence could be achieved within a relatively short period. However, limitations in computing power, data availability, memory capacity, and algorithmic efficiency restricted further progress. During the 1970s and 1980s, Artificial Intelligence experienced periods commonly known as the "AI Winters," characterized by reduced research funding, slower technological progress, and diminished public expectations. Many ambitious predictions regarding human-level machine intelligence proved unrealistic because available computing resources and algorithms were insufficient to support increasingly complex AI applications. Despite these challenges, important research continued in knowledge representation, expert systems, machine learning, robotics, and computational reasoning. Expert systems became particularly successful by capturing specialized human knowledge through rule-based decision-making frameworks that supported medical diagnosis, engineering design, financial analysis, and industrial management.The late 1980s and 1990s marked the gradual resurgence of Artificial Intelligence through the development of machine learning approaches. Rather than relying exclusively on manually programmed rules, researchers began designing algorithms capable of learning patterns directly from data. Statistical modelling, neural networks, evolutionary computation, fuzzy logic, probabilistic reasoning, and support vector machines expanded the capabilities of intelligent systems while improving adaptability, prediction accuracy, and decision-making performance. Significant improvements in computational hardware further accelerated AI research during this period. A landmark achievement occurred in 1997 when IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, demonstrating the ability of intelligent computing systems to outperform human experts in highly specialized domains. This achievement attracted worldwide attention and illustrated the practical potential of Artificial Intelligence beyond theoretical research. Similar advances subsequently appeared in speech recognition, computer vision, autonomous robotics, medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and industrial automation.The twenty-first century has witnessed unprecedented growth in Artificial Intelligence driven by three major technological developments: the availability of massive digital datasets, substantial improvements in computational processing power, and the emergence of advanced machine learning algorithms. The rapid expansion of the internet, cloud computing, mobile technologies, social media, and digital services generated enormous volumes of data that enabled intelligent systems to learn more effectively. Simultaneously, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), high-performance computing, and cloud-based infrastructure significantly accelerated AI model training and deployment across diverse application domains. Deep learning has become one of the most influential developments in contemporary Artificial Intelligence. Inspired by the structure of the human brain, deep neural networks consist of multiple computational layers capable of learning complex representations from large datasets. These architectures have dramatically improved performance in image recognition, speech processing, language translation, autonomous driving, medical imaging, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and scientific research. Deep learning has transformed Artificial Intelligence from narrow task-specific applications into highly sophisticated systems capable of addressing increasingly complex real-world challenges.Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced remarkable advancement through transformer architectures and large language models capable of understanding, generating, summarizing, translating, and analysing human language with unprecedented accuracy. Conversational AI systems, intelligent virtual assistants, multilingual communication platforms, automated content generation, and research support tools have become integral components of education, healthcare, business, governance, and scientific research. These developments have substantially enhanced human-computer interaction while expanding opportunities for intelligent educational technologies. The emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence represents another significant milestone in AI evolution. Modern generative models can produce text, images, computer code, audio, video, simulations, educational content, and scientific documentation while supporting creativity, innovation, research, and personalized learning. These technologies have transformed knowledge creation and digital communication by enabling collaborative interactions between humans and intelligent systems across numerous professional disciplines.Artificial Intelligence has evolved beyond isolated computational applications into a foundational technology supporting digital transformation across multiple sectors. Healthcare employs AI for disease diagnosis, medical imaging, drug discovery, personalized treatment, and patient monitoring. Manufacturing integrates AI with robotics, predictive maintenance, quality control, and smart production systems. Financial institutions utilize intelligent algorithms for fraud detection, risk management, investment analysis, and customer services. Agriculture benefits from precision farming, crop monitoring, environmental analysis, and resource optimization. Transportation increasingly relies upon autonomous vehicles, intelligent traffic management, and logistics optimization. Education has emerged as one of the fastest-growing application areas where Artificial Intelligence supports personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, curriculum development, learning analytics, educational administration, and lifelong learning. documents.abstract: BackgroundThe increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into workplace practices has reshaped how employees process information and perform cognitive tasks. While these systems are often associated with superior efficiency, their excessive use may entail significant cognitive costs.ObjectiveGrounded in automation complacency perspective and the growing literature on technology addiction, this study investigates how dependence on artificial intelligence is associated with cognitive engagement in the workplace, with particular attention to the mediating role of cognitive fatigue.MethodsAdopting quantitative research design, data were collected from 246 academic and administrative staff who actively use AI tools in their daily work routines. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the theoretical model proposed.ResultsThe findings indicate that dependence on AI was positively associated with cognitive fatigue (β = 0.569; t = 13.468; p = 0.000) and negatively with cognitive engagement (β = -0.174; t = 2.503; p = 0.012). In addition, the relationship between cognitive fatigue and cognitive engagement was found to be negative and statistically significant (β = -0.207; t = 2.773; p = 0.006). Mediation analysis further revealed that cognitive fatigue partially mediates the relationship between dependence on AI and cognitive engagement (indirect effect β = -0.118, t = 2.724, p < .01; VAF = 40.5%).ConclusionThese results suggest that higher levels of dependence on AI correspond to higher employee cognitive fatigue, which in turn relates to lower cognitive engagement at work. By empirically demonstrating the cognitive costs of AI reliance, this study contributes to the emerging literature on workplace AI and technology addiction.

Abstract This study examines the transition from automation to generative AI in professional communication, focusing on human–AI co-creativity. While earlier research framed AI mainly as an efficiency tool, the rapid emergence of generative AI has reconfigured communication practices toward collaborative and co-creative models. This structured literature synthesis, informed by PRISMA reporting principles, synthesizes empirical research published between 2012 and 2026 across journalism, public relations, strategic communication, and digital media, investigating how generative AI is integrated into creative workflows and how communicative agency is distributed between human professionals and AI systems. The results identify four dimensions shaping human–AI co-creativity: (1) AI affordances enabling ideation while introducing constraints such as algorithmic opacity; (2) human professional agency, through which practitioners retain interpretive authority via prompt design; (3) organizational context, structuring AI adoption; and (4) ethical and cultural norms concerning transparency and accountability. The review advances conceptual clarity on human–AI co-creativity as an emergent sociotechnical process, arguing that generative AI is not simply augmenting communication work but fundamentally reshaping how creativity, authorship, and responsibility are enacted. documents.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence–driven chatbots into digital commerce has transformed firm–consumer interactions, shifting the focus from efficiency-oriented automation toward more human-centered engagement. In this context, anthropomorphic chatbot design has emerged as a key mechanism through which firms seek to introduce human touch into AI-mediated interactions and influence consumer purchase intention. Despite growing scholarly attention, existing research on chatbot anthropomorphism remains fragmented across disciplines, limiting a comprehensive understanding of its intellectual structure, theoretical foundations, and thematic evolution. To address this gap, the present study conducts a PRISMA 2020–guided bibliometric and systematic review of research published between 2016 and 2025. Drawing on a bibliometric dataset of 200 publications and a systematically screened subset of 80 high-quality studies, the analysis employs VOSviewer to examine publication trends, keyword co-occurrence patterns, and co-authorship networks. The findings reveal a clear progression in the literature from automation-focused chatbot applications toward human-centered AI interactions emphasizing anthropomorphism, social presence, and relational mechanisms. The results identify anthropomorphic design, human touch, trust, and consumer engagement as central themes shaping purchase intention in chatbot-mediated environments. By integrating anthropomorphism theory, social presence theory, and the Computers as Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, the study proposes a theory-driven framework explaining how human-like chatbot cues activate perceptions of human touch, which subsequently foster trust and influence consumer buying behavior. Beyond consolidating fragmented literature, this study advances theoretical understanding of human-centered AI and offers actionable insights for managers seeking to design effective chatbot interactions in digital commerce. The findings also highlight promising avenues for future research, including contextual, cross cultural, and ethical considerations in anthropomorphic AI design.

The transformation of knowledge from the classical Islamic tradition to the modern era and Artificial Intelligence (AI) demonstrates not only the growth of knowledge but also shifts in its sources, methods, validity, and authority. However, studies on Bayt al-Hikmah, the development of modern science, Islamic epistemology, and AI in Islamic education tend to be discussed in separate domains. Consequently, the connection between these epistemological transformations and scientific integration in Islamic education has not been systematically examined. This study aims to analyze the epistemological transformation of knowledge from classical scholarly traditions through Bayt al-Hikmah, the development of modern science, to the AI era, and to examine its relevance to scientific integration in Islamic education. This study employs a qualitative approach with a library research method. Literature was analyzed descriptively and analytically across four dimensions: sources, methods, validity, and authority of knowledge. The findings indicate that Bayt al-Hikmah represents an open scientific paradigm toward various traditions through translation, dialogue, critique, and knowledge development. Modern science subsequently reinforced scientific methods, observation, experimentation, and empirical proof, though the rise of specialization also risks driving scientific fragmentation. The contribution of this study lies in its continuous reading of these transformations through four epistemological dimensions and their connection to the integrative-interconnective paradigm in Islamic education. In this context, scientific integration needs to connect revelation, reason, empirical experience, technology, and ethical and spiritual values. AI should be positioned as an instrument for knowledge development that remains subject to human verification, interpretation, and ethical judgment.

This work presents a theoretical architecture for continually adapting AI systems organized around three distinct timescales: (1) fast transformer key-value context for immediate interaction, (2) medium-term persistent recurrent memory with decaying importance and consolidation, and (3) slow, controlled parameter adaptation. The proposed pathway is context → persistent memory → importance estimation → consolidation → plasticity gating → bounded parameter update → changed future computation. The manuscript formalizes recurrent state dynamics, transformer attention, gated persistent memory, exponential importance decay, importance-biased retrieval, prediction loss, gated online updates, consolidation thresholds, and learned update rules. It also explains why adapting recurrent transition weights such as U changes state-transition dynamics, whereas updating memory changes stored state without necessarily changing the underlying transition rule. The package distinguishes inference-time state adaptation, memory adaptation, online parameter learning, meta-learning, recursive self-learning, and recursive self-improvement. It proposes controlled experiments comparing transformer, KV-context, persistent-memory, importance, consolidation, gated-update, and learned-update variants, with metrics for retention, transfer, forgetting, poisoning robustness, parameter drift, retrieval quality, and compute cost. This is a conceptual research architecture and falsifiable research hypothesis. It reports no experimental measurements and does not claim AGI, consciousness, human-level cognition, biological equivalence, or open-ended recursive self-improvement. The prefrontal-cortex comparison is functional only, referring to working-memory maintenance, goal persistence, error monitoring, and adaptive control. Final authorship and publication decisions remain with Chaman Prakash Kanth. Sarvam AI was also used.

documents.abstract: Literature is a mirror of society. It shows the economic conditions, social problems, and daily struggles of human life across different times. Work is one of the most important parts of human life. In the past, many people depended completely on land, rich masters, or family heads for their survival. Over time, the meaning of work has changed from total dependence to economic independence. English literature presents many stories of characters who fight against poverty and social rules to earn their own living and live with dignity. Work is not just a way to earn money; it also gives a person self-respect, identity, and personal freedom. This research paper examines how work, economy, and independence are presented in selected English literary texts: Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre, Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South, and Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own. These texts show how education, employment, and money help individuals to become free and confident. Finally, this paper connects these literary lessons with the modern world. Today, technology, artificial intelligence, online platforms, and work-from-home jobs are changing the future of work. The paper concludes that even in the modern digital age, human dignity and economic security are essential for true freedom.

Abstract India’s vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 requires a digital governance architecture that can transform rapidly expanding volumes of public data into timely, evidence-based, inclusive, transparent, and sustainable policy outcomes. This paper develops an integrated conceptual framework for data-driven digital governance by examining the complementary roles of Data Analytics, Business Intelligence (BI), Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), and Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI). Drawing on conceptual analysis and secondary evidence, the study conceptualizes DPI as the foundational layer for interoperable and trusted digital services, while Data Analytics and BI enable the transformation of data into descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive intelligence. Responsible AI further strengthens forecasting, simulation, decision support, and adaptive governance while incorporating principles of transparency, accountability, privacy, fairness, security, and human oversight. A key contribution of the study is the proposed six-level BI maturity model, progressing from Digitization and Reporting to Diagnostic BI, Predictive Analytics, Decision Intelligence, and Adaptive Governance. The model addresses the challenge of dashboard-oriented governance by emphasising the progression from data availability to actionable intelligence, informed decision-making, outcome measurement, and continuous policy feedback. The study also identifies critical barriers, including data fragmentation, interoperability constraints, privacy and cybersecurity risks, algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, institutional capability gaps, and inadequate outcome measurement. To address these challenges, a phased 2027–2047 strategic roadmap is proposed, beginning with common data standards and institutional analytics capacity and progressing toward interoperable, AI-assisted, outcome-oriented, and continuously learning governance systems. The paper argues that India’s long-term digital governance advantage will depend not merely on achieving digitalization at population scale, but on developing the institutional and technological capacity to convert data into intelligence, intelligence into informed decisions, and decisions into measurable and inclusive public value.

A key contribution of the study is the proposed six-level BI maturity model, progressing from Digitization and Reporting to Diagnostic BI, Predictive Analytics, Decision Intelligence, and Adaptive Governance. The model addresses the challenge of dashboard-oriented governance by emphasising the progression from data availability to actionable intelligence, informed decision-making, outcome measurement, and continuous policy feedback. The study also identifies critical barriers, including data fragmentation, interoperability constraints, privacy and cybersecurity risks, algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, institutional capability gaps, and inadequate outcome measurement. To address these challenges, a phased 2027–2047 strategic roadmap is proposed, beginning with common data standards and institutional analytics capacity and progressing toward interoperable, AI-assisted, outcome-oriented, and continuously learning governance systems. The paper argues that India’s long-term digital governance advantage will depend not merely on achieving digitalization at population scale, but on developing the institutional and technological capacity to convert data into intelligence, intelligence into informed decisions, and decisions into measurable and inclusive public value.

documents.abstract: Abstract : Gatekeeping has remained one of the foundational theoretical approaches for explaining how information becomes news. From Kurt Lewin’s conceptualisation of gates and channels to David Manning White’s study of the newspaper wire editor, traditional gatekeeping theory located considerable power in human actors who selected, rejected and organised information before it reached audiences. The contemporary news environment, however, complicates this model. News selection is increasingly distributed across journalists, newsroom analytics, search engines, social media platforms, recommender systems and generative artificial intelligence. This paper re-examines gatekeeping theory through an interdisciplinary synthesis of journalism studies, platform studies, artificial intelligence research and communication theory. Drawing on a structured conceptual review of more than 29 major scholarly contributions, it argues that contemporary journalism is moving from identifiable gatekeepers towards interconnected gatekeeping systems. Within these systems, editorial judgement has not disappeared; rather, it interacts continuously with computational selection, platform infrastructures, audience behaviour and generative systems capable of producing, summarising and reorganising information. The paper proposes a five-layer model of contemporary gatekeeping comprising source, editorial, algorithmic, platform and generative gates. It further distinguishes between selection power, traditionally exercised by editors, and visibility power, increasingly exercised through technological infrastructures. The study concludes that gatekeeping theory remains valuable but requires conceptual expansion from the question of who controls the gate to the broader question of how interconnected human and computational systems determine what information becomes visible, credible and socially consequential.

Purpose This study aims to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enabled knowledge creation processes influence entrepreneurial knowledge co-creation and small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) digital transformation through entrepreneurial general innovativeness and entrepreneurial specific innovativeness. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the socialization, externalization, combination and internalization (SECI) knowledge creation framework, the study develops and tests a mediation model linking GenAI internalization (GAI), GenAI externalization (GAE), GenAI socialization (GAS) and GenAI combination (GAC) with SME outcomes. Data was collected from 391 SME respondents and analysed using covariance-based structural equation modelling in analysis of moment structures. Findings The findings show that GAI, GAE and GAC significantly enhance both entrepreneurial general innovativeness and entrepreneurial specific innovativeness. GAS significantly influences entrepreneurial specific innovativeness but does not significantly affect entrepreneurial general innovativeness. Both forms of entrepreneurial innovativeness positively influence entrepreneurial knowledge co-creation and SME digital transformation. Mediation results further show that entrepreneurial general innovativeness mediates the effects of GAI, GAE and GAC, while entrepreneurial specific innovativeness provides a more consistent mediating pathway across GenAI-enabled knowledge processes. Practical implications SME managers should use GenAI not merely for automation or content generation, but for learning, knowledge articulation, knowledge integration, innovation adoption and digital transformation. Originality/value The study advances GenAI entrepreneurship research by showing how GenAI-enabled SECI processes create SME value through entrepreneurial innovativeness.

Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Opportunistic screening using routinely acquired clinical data offers a scalable approach for identifying high-risk individuals before acute events occur. Although chest X-rays (CXRs) capture latent cardiovascular biomarkers and clinical histories provide complementary patient context, existing medical vision-language models are primarily optimized for radiology interpretation rather than prognostic reasoning. We propose a causal reinforcement learning framework for multimodal clinical reasoning that integrates CXRs and physician-authored clinical histories for opportunistic MACE prediction. The framework introduces (1) a role-decoupled dual-LLM architecture that separates reasoning from risk prediction, (2) a dual-action causal reinforcement learning policy for evidence selection and reasoning optimization, and (3) causal token pruning to learn compact multimodal representations. Evaluated on an internal cohort, an emergency department cohort, and the external MIMIC dataset, the proposed framework consistently outperformed unimodal baselines and state-of-the-art medical vision-language models, achieving AUROCs of 0.720, 0.760, and 0.845, respectively. It also substantially improved reasoning quality, achieving higher GREEN scores and higher expert preference while maintaining robust predictive performance across diverse patient populations.

documents.abstract: Abstract In recent years, the groundbreaking development of AI technologies such as text-to-image generation has revealed the unprecedented potential of machines in the realm of artistic creation. This has reignited and intensified widespread reflections on historical issues in artistic practice, including ontological questions, the identity of the author, the configuration of human–machine relationships, and the positioning of creativity. To address these concerns, this paper mainly seeks to draw inspiration from the important artistic thoughts of two conceptual artists who were active in the 1960s: Yoko Ono and Sol LeWitt. It also explores the interconnectedness and continuity between generative AI art practices and the legacy of conceptual art, tracing the historical trajectory of the relationship between conceptual art and digital art. Beyond the pivotal artistic practices of these two pioneering conceptual artists, the comparative analysis also encompasses the examination of additional associated artistic endeavors in relation to text-guided image synthesis. This broader scope of artists aims to more comprehensively support the argument on the impact of artificial intelligence on participatory frameworks and the concept of authorship within future creative practices. By delving into a discussion on dematerialization with conceptual art’s focus on concepts over material objects, the authors explore the potential for a posthumanist paradigm in AI art practices, to consider the reconfiguration of creativity in human–machine collaborations. Through speculative explorations of AI visualizations of Ono's and LeWitt's instructions and evaluating the role of "prompt engineering" in collaborative creation, new forms of distributed creativity that respond to posthumanist provocations are discovered. Leveraging the posthumanist emphasis on the “biological and microbiological entanglement with nonhumans”, this approach aids in dislodging the centrality of the individual or the artist within the creative process (Herbrechter 2023, p. 8). This critical examination highlights the disruptive potential of conceptual art in reshaping the notion of authorship within its symbiotic relationship with technological culture. It reveals the dynamic and co-evolutionary relationship between the conceptual art discourse and its reinterpretation within the emerging computational participatory structures of the artistic frontier. By drawing on the legacy of conceptual art, this study attempts to reconcile the tensions between conceptual completion, technological participation, artistic ontology, and distributed creativity, providing theoretical support for current AI art practices and driving the ongoing reconsideration of posthuman creative partnerships in technology mediated artistic production.

Despite being an emerging credible means of using artificial intelligence (AI) for improving disease surveillance via early detection of outbreaks, epidemics prediction and evidence-based decision-making, there continue to be challenges in the use of AI tools in many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) due to various factors including fragmented health information system, digital inequality, governance problems and institutional incapability. Most of the research conducted so far has concentrated on the efficacy and accuracy of AI in terms of predicting outbreaks, with little focus on other conditions necessary for its deployment. This study adopts a qualitative problem-discovery research design, integrating thematic analysis with philosophical analysis to examine the structural and normative barriers surrounding AI implementation in disease surveillance. The analysis identifies four interrelated dimensions of implementation readiness: epistemic adequacy, distributive justice, ethics of governance, and institutional legitimacy. These dimensions provide a framework for understanding how limitations in knowledge integration, unequal digital infrastructure, privacy and accountability concerns, and deficits in institutional and public trust can constrain the practical adoption of AI-enabled surveillance. Rather than proposing another predictive model, this study develops a theoretical framework that conceptualizes AI implementation in disease surveillance as simultaneously a socio-technical and normative process. The framework provides a foundation for subsequent empirical investigation and offers a structured perspective for designing more context-sensitive, ethically grounded, and institutionally sustainable AI-enabled disease surveillance systems in resource-constrained healthcare settings.

This working paper develops the worldwide normative claim of Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NMR) and semantic field. It examines how an organismic understanding of human life, basic needs and collective problem-solving can inform standards for education, institutions, community development and human-AI cooperation. The argument makes the normative bridge explicit: when the preservation and flourishing of human life, equal consideration of persons and the protection of shared life-supporting conditions are accepted as aims, societal decisions should be assessed by their effects on those conditions. The six NMR domains are thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realization and participation, and meaning. The New Human Rights articulate rights and aims; the semantic field provides a connected vocabulary for understanding situations, evaluating alternatives and organizing cooperative action. What this article adds:Normative orientation is already present in the existing framework. This paper’s specific contribution is its focused justification of worldwide normative use. It distinguishes anthropological description, normative commitments and institutional implications, and illustrates their connection through the participatory redesign of a public square. Function within the Zenodo corpus:The article connects the reconstruction of Martin’s theory architecture with public justification and practical decision criteria. It links existing strands on Learning by Teaching, New Human Rights, semantic coherence, prioritization, governance and human-AI cooperation. It thus serves as a bridge from conceptual synthesis to accountable societal application. Worldwide orientation is understood as shared evaluative concerns combined with context-sensitive implementation. The paper proposes a framework for public discussion and application; it does not claim existing international endorsement or legal recognition of the NMR. This is a conceptual working paper without a new empirical dataset. Jean-Pol Martin supplied the conceptual framework and direction. ChatGPT assisted with argument development, English drafting and layout.

documents.abstract: Many of the most valuable scientific datasets cannot be centralized: they are proprietary, export-controlled, classified, or bound by data-sovereignty restrictions. This inverts the usual paradigm: the model must move to the data, making federated artificial intelligence (AI) core infrastructure for open science. We synthesize lessons from U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories, industry deployments, and the open-source community into a structured account of moving federated AI from pilot demonstrations to dependable, multi-site production. The lessons come from five concurrent efforts spanning leadership-class supercomputers and cloud infrastructure in regulated settings. We organize them around an adapted \textit{five-domain readiness frame} and a stratified view of the stack beneath a trained model: data architecture, privacy and security controls, trust and verification, governance and socio-technical factors, and operations, the layers that decide whether a pilot becomes dependable. The question shifts from ``can we train it?'' to ``can we operate it, audit it, and change it safely?'' We report systems lessons in memory efficiency, reliability, and synchronization; set out what privacy, security, and decentralized trust require in production, and what is not yet validated there; and identify cross-cutting open problems (asynchronous federation, leakage auditing, verification standards, and harmonized data contracts) that we argue warrant a dedicated, international, open-science working group.

Current ride-sharing platforms predominantly rely on subjective post-ride ratings to evaluate driver credibility, making reputation systems vulnerable to user bias, delayed feedback, collusion, and manipulation. Although recent studies have explored blockchain-based ride-sharing, AI-driven driver monitoring, and IoT-enabled transportation independently, they do not provide an integrated trust framework that continuously derives credibility from objectively verifiable driving behaviour while maintaining scalability and low operational cost.This paper presents Ridezy, a decentralized trust architecture that replaces conventional rating-based reputation with real-time sensor-driven credibility. The proposed framework combines edge Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things (AIIoT) technologies to continuously monitor behavioural indicators such as lane discipline, speed compliance, braking behaviour, and traffic sign adherence. Instead of storing high-frequency telemetry on the blockchain, Ridezy employs a hybrid architecture in which behavioural summaries are processed off-chain and only cryptographic hashes, credibility updates, and payment records are anchored on Polygon smart contracts, enabling tamper-evident trust with minimal blockchain overhead. To evaluate the proposed architecture, Ridezy is compared against three representative trust models: a traditional rating-based system, an AI-only architecture, and a blockchain-only architecture. The evaluation considers behavioural detection performance, end-to-end latency, cost efficiency, throughput, reputation stability, tamper resistance, and component-wise ablation studies. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid architecture achieves higher behavioural fidelity and stronger trust guarantees than conventional reputation mechanisms while maintaining low per-ride blockchain cost and scalable operation through batched on-chain commitments.The primary contribution of this work is a sensor-driven credibility framework that transforms real-time behavioural evidence into a cryptographically verifiable trust primitive for ride-sharing ecosystems. By combining edge AI, IoT telemetry, and blockchain-based trust anchoring within a scalable hybrid architecture, Ridezy provides a practical foundation for trustworthy, transparent, and next-generation intelligent mobility systems.

documents.abstract: AI is rapidly transforming the educational landscape, and its future impact is expected to extend beyond individual learning tools toward broader changes in teaching, assessment, institutional management, research, and educational ecosystems. Future developments may create increasingly intelligent and personalized learning environments in which humans and AI systems work together to support educational goals. The year 2035 represents an important horizon for considering the future development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education. By this period, AI may become deeply integrated into learning platforms, educational administration, research environments, assessment systems, digital classrooms, and professional education. The future of education is unlikely to be based on AI alone. Instead, educational environments may increasingly combine AI capabilities with human expertise, creativity, emotional intelligence, critical thinking, and ethical responsibility. A possible framework is: AI Technology + Human Expertise + Digital Infrastructure + Ethical Governance = Future Education By 2035, AI may become a regular component of educational environments rather than an additional technological tool. Students may interact with intelligent learning systems that continuously adapt to their learning progress, interests, abilities, and educational goals. Teachers may use AI to support lesson planning, assessment, learning analytics, content development, and personalized instruction.

documents.abstract: The article proposes a fuzzy model for assessing the level of digital security literacy of the population, considering socio-demographic characteristics. The relevance of the study is determined by the growth of cyber threats, digital risks, and the role of the human factor in ensuring the stability of the digital environment, which requires a transition from fragmentary measurements to comprehensive and interpretable assessment approaches. The scientific novelty of the work lies in combining the convolution method and fuzzy modelling to form integral quantitative and linguistic assessments of digital security literacy across various social profiles of the population. The proposed method makes it possible to formalize heterogeneous demographic and behavioural data, conduct profile-based analysis, and generate targeted analytical conclusions to support management decision-making. The practical significance of the study was confirmed by verifying the proposed method on real empirical data obtained from a questionnaire survey of 315 respondents in the Transcarpathian region. The verification showed that the proposed method provides a normalized quantitative assessment for a selected social profile with an integral value of 0.644, which corresponds to an above-average level of digital security literacy. Compared with simple averaging of the entire sample, the proposed method increases the analytical specificity of the assessment by enabling profile-oriented evaluation and targeted interpretation of results rather than only obtaining a generalized population-level indicator. The results obtained demonstrate the possibility of using the proposed method to assess the level of digital security literacy, segment the population by social profiles, identify vulnerable groups, and justify targeted educational and preventive measures. Prospects for further research are related to expanding the empirical base, automating data collection and processing procedures, integrating new assessment criteria, and analysing the dynamics of digital security literacy over time and across regions.

We present FYAN, a human--AI harness for document-level mathematical formalization. Rather than treating theorems in isolation, FYAN coordinates an end-to-end workflow spanning specification, proof planning, logical review, Lean proof construction, knowledge curation, and validation, with support for independent supervision and human guidance. A central component is evidence-grounded semantic auditing, which assesses whether formal statements faithfully preserve their informal specifications. A language model constructs structured evidence over local correspondences, omissions, scope, and logical relations, while a deterministic validator checks this evidence and produces reproducible judgments. When a substantive but admissible deviation is accepted, FYAN requires an explicit proof-transfer obligation connecting the formal statement back to a source-facing interpretation. With the same model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) in every stage, FYAN proves 86 of 143 FormalTCS theorems under a strict Lean check, against 69 for a general agent harness, and raises the natural-language proof score from 0.501 to 0.851. On ConsistencyCheck, its semantic audit catches more inconsistent statements than a direct LLM judge, both on labels verified against the source (recall 0.777 vs. 0.636) and on the original labels (0.873 vs. 0.820), and localizes each mismatch it reports to a specific hypothesis, conclusion, or scope. FYAN also built ODENumLib, a 9,355-line Lean library for the numerical analysis of ordinary differential equation.

Abstract Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by difficulties in social communication and interaction, together with restricted or repetitive patterns of behavior. Early screening is important for facilitating timely clinical assessment and intervention; however, conventional screening approaches often depend on clinical expertise, behavioral observation, developmental history, and standardized assessment tools. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have created new opportunities for data-driven and automated ASD screening. This survey provides a comprehensive review of AI-based approaches for ASD screening, with particular emphasis on multimodal learning and the integration of heterogeneous data sources. Behavioral, genetic, environmental, neuroimaging, physiological, and clinical data modalities are examined, along with approaches for combining information across multiple sources. The survey further reviews the role of GANs and related generative approaches in synthetic-data generation and data augmentation, particularly in addressing challenges associated with limited and imbalanced datasets. Multimodal fusion strategies, multi-input neural networks, and emerging deep learning approaches are also discussed in the context of ASD screening. The reviewed literature indicates that multimodal AI has the potential to provide a more comprehensive representation of ASD-related characteristics than single-modality approaches. However, important challenges remain, including limited and heterogeneous datasets, class imbalance, multimodal data integration, GAN training instability, synthetic-data quality, privacy and security, model interpretability, generalizability, and limited external clinical validation. This survey identifies these challenges and highlights research directions toward reliable, explainable, privacy-preserving, and clinically validated AI-based multimodal ASD screening systems. Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs); Multimodal Learning; ASD Screening; Data Augmentation; Synthetic Data

Biomolecular networks underlie both natural biological processes and engineered cellular technologies, from intracellular regulation and ecological dynamics to biomanufacturing, smart therapeutics, and cell-based diagnostics. However, designing chemical reaction networks (CRNs) that implement a desired dynamical function remains a challenging task. Although candidate networks can be evaluated by simulation, the inverse problem of discovering networks from behavioral specifications remains difficult. It requires navigating vast spaces of topologies and kinetic parameters governed by nonlinear and potentially stochastic dynamics. Here, we introduce GenAI-Net, a generative artificial intelligence framework that automates CRN design by coupling reaction proposal to simulation-based evaluation defined by a user-specified objective. GenAI-Net efficiently produces topologically diverse solutions across design tasks, including dose-response shaping, complex logic gates, classifiers, oscillators, habituation, robust perfect adaptation, and noise reduction in stochastic settings. By turning specifications into families of circuit candidates, GenAI-Net provides a route to programmable biomolecular circuit design and accelerates translation from desired function to implementable mechanisms.

Abstract The rapid emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is creating new opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve business processes, innovation, productivity, and competitiveness. However, the factors encouraging or limiting Generative AI adoption and its performance outcomes among SMEs in Nigeria remain underexplored. This study examines Generative AI adoption by SMEs in Nigeria, focusing on its drivers, barriers, and performance outcomes. A cross-sectional survey research design was employed, with data collected from 200 SME owners, managers, and employees using a structured questionnaire titled Generative AI Adoption and SME Performance Questionnaire (GAIA-SPQ), validated with a reliability coefficient of 0.86. Data were analyzed using correlation analysis at a 0.05 level of significance. Findings reveal that drivers of Generative AI significantly influence its adoption, while barriers also significantly affect adoption negatively. The study further finds that Generative AI use significantly affects SME performance, particularly in relation to productivity and innovation. The study concludes that Generative AI provides important opportunities for improving SME performance, although effective adoption requires favourable conditions and the reduction of implementation barriers. It is recommended that SMEs strengthen their technological capabilities, develop relevant digital skills, and adopt cost-effective Generative AI solutions to improve productivity, innovation, and competitiveness.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered Islamic schools, seminaries and universities faster than the institutions can govern it. Students use chatbots to explain verses, draft essays and prepare for examinations, while teachers lack shared rules on what is permitted, how to disclose it and how to assess learning fairly. This paper proposes a practical framework that grounds those decisions in the objectives of the Sharia (maqāṣid al-sharīʿa) rather than in generic ethics alone. Using an analytical synthesis of recent evidence on generative AI in education, research on assessment and academic integrity, international governance guidance, and the maqāṣid literature, the paper maps the five classical necessities (religion, life, intellect, lineage and property) onto the risks of AI-mediated learning and derives design principles for three layers: curriculum, assessment and academic integrity. The framework calls for AI literacy grounded in the ethic of verification, assessment built on authentic and oral demonstration of understanding instead of unreliable detection software, a three-tier policy on permitted use with disclosure, and governance that protects learner data and religious content. A phased implementation route and indicators are offered for institutions. The paper is conceptual and untested in practice; it closes with a research agenda for piloting the framework, comparing it across legal schools and measuring its effects on learning.

Background. The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education has created challenges in designing responsible and adaptive learning strategies. Meanwhile, competitive elements in gamified learning remain debated due to inconsistent effects on learner engagement. Purpose. This research aimed to develop and evaluate a generative AI-assisted competitive microlearning strategy for improving instructional media development skills among Finnish Luokanopettajakoulutus (Class Teacher Education) students. Novelty. This study introduces a novel instructional design that integrates generative AI, microlearning, and optional quality-based competition. Unlike conventional competitive gamification approaches, the proposed strategy recognizes learner differences by examining whether competition produces varied outcomes across learning groups Method. Using the Plomp development model, the study involved 79 undergraduate students from four parallel classes. Data from expert validation, practicality questionnaires, and product assessments were analyzed using Aiken’s V and descriptive statistics. Results. The strategy achieved high validity (Aiken’s V = 0.87) and strong practicality (83.1% student response; 85.9% lecturer response). Variation in competition participation (41–62%) indicated different effects among learner groups. Conclusion. The findings contribute an adaptive AI-assisted microlearning framework that balances innovation, learner diversity, and educational equity in teacher education.

documents.abstract: The way we distribute research data and software today relies heavily on the open web: largely standardised formats, decentralised data hubs, public availability, affordable compute, free learning resources, and findability afforded by a few ad-supported web indexes. This openness, however, is increasingly under threat. The companies that currently attempt to monetise large language models also make it much harder to keep websites online and position their chat interfaces as intermediaries between knowledge and users. The ‘AI’-enclosed web empowers Big Tech to further interfere in learning, education, and research. This talk draws a parallel to the historical appropriation of common land in 18th- and 19th-century England. With this historical revolution of the rich against the poor to learn from, it outlines the specific dangers to the knowledge commons in the next few years. In conclusion, the talk attempts to identify what can be done to preserve and and empower individual, institutional, and transnational data sovereignty in the face of this not entirely new threat: critique the neoreactionary ideology behind the technology, empower ‘boring’ technology, identify affordable machine-learning tech, and embrace local and peer-to-peer computing.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems coordinate specialized reasoning through aggregation, interaction, and adaptive control, yet their potential for graph learning remains unexplored. Graph learning is a natural setting for such systems because useful evidence may arise from heterogeneous local, long-range, global structural, and semantic perspectives whose relevance varies across instances. Existing LLM-based graph learning approaches primarily rely on single-agent reasoning, while multi-agent coordination has been studied mainly in general reasoning settings. Consequently, it remains unclear whether multiple specialized agents can improve graph learning and how coordination strategies should be designed and evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMAS, a systematic benchmark of multi-agent coordination for graph learning. GraphMAS builds a shared pool of graph reasoning specialists and organizes coordination along two dimensions, inter-agent interaction and runtime adaptivity, yielding four paradigms and seven representative coordination methods. Under a unified protocol, we evaluate these methods across seven text-attributed graphs, three domains, and two graph learning tasks. We find that heterogeneous graph perspectives are complementary, and that coordinating specialists improves over individual specialists and single-agent graph reasoning, with gains from decomposing reasoning across specialists rather than from broader evidence access alone. However, richer inter-agent interaction does not reliably help, whereas instance-adaptive specialist selection yields the strongest accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We further show that coordination can be learned over a fixed specialist pool and transfers to held-out graphs. GraphMAS therefore provides a controlled evaluation framework and empirical principles for understanding when and how multi-agent coordination benefits graph learning.

Physical culture, as a subcomponent of general culture, reflects the set of constructive manifestations of the human factor in the field of movement, integrating the progress of science, technology, art and medicine (Platonov, Vl., 2006). Within this theoretical framework, the present study aims to show the historical continuity and practical evolution of Greco-Roman wrestling as a specific expression of physical culture, analyzing the connections between socio-cultural development, advances in biomotor sciences and transformations of modern pedagogical paradigms. The paper offers an analytical approach that goes beyond general terminological observations, bringing the following contributions: 1) identifying the historical and socio-cultural stages that shaped the forms and functions of Greco-Roman wrestling; 2) integrating empirical evidence from biomotricity to explain the technical-tactical adaptations and physiological requirements of athletes; 3) formulating contemporary pedagogical directions for optimizing the technical-tactical and physical preparation process within combat training. Thus, the paper argues for the continuity of a specific sports tradition within the broader framework of physical culture and proposes practical and theoretical frameworks for integrating historical knowledge into the design of training and sports education programs.

documents.abstract: Precise grounding matters. It specifies which object is the target and where that object is, even in clutter and for tiny objects, and it has to be fast enough for closed-loop control. Yet vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) take perception from general-purpose vision-language and video-generation backbones, which still fail in these settings. We introduce GroundingPI, a 4B grounding foundation model that generates points and boxes as quantized coordinates in a shared vocabulary. Training combines multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO, using supervision from public datasets and dedicated data engines. Against 44 baselines across 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, GroundingPI establishes a new state of the art, averaging 73.68%, above the larger GPT-6 Astra (71.54%). As a downstream visual backbone, GroundingPI improves performance on robotic manipulation and autonomous driving. On RoboTwin 2.0, it outperforms every mainstream backbone we evaluate in all four out-of-distribution settings, by up to 24.8% relative to the strongest backbone. On RoboCasa-GR1, GroundingPI trained with 50% of the demonstrations outperforms those baselines trained with 75%. On nuScenes, used as the visual backbone, GroundingPI attains an average open-loop L2 error of 0.296 m. We systematically analyze GroundingPI's pretraining in scale and data composition. Downstream autonomous driving and robotic manipulation improve as the pretraining is scaled. Analyzing the data recipe across these 11 perceptual capabilities shows dense grounding's substantial benefits for both, and OCR's potential as a catalyst for perceptual learning. These results support grounding as a perceptual foundation, and dedicated perceptual pretraining as a promising direction for foundation models of physical intelligence.

documents.abstract: The proliferation of smart devices exposes children to online risks like grooming and financial scams that are deeply embedded within legitimate applications. Current approaches rely on automated prevention and detection, a paradigm that is fundamentally limited by its inherent fallibility. Whether rule-based or AI-driven, they inevitably produce false positives and negatives, failing to provide reliable protection. In this paper, we argue for a complementary, human-in-the-loop, post-hoc forensic paradigm. We present GUIA uditor , the first system designed to realize this vision by creating GUI Provenance: a queryable, semantic record of a child's interaction sequence. To generate this, GUIA uditor leverages a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to translate the temporal sequence of GUI events into a human-understandable narrative. To make this practical on mobile devices, a novel evidence distillation pipeline reduces the data requiring analysis by over 89.2% compared to periodic sampling approaches adopted by industry standards, with negligible impact on accuracy. On a new dataset of 295 interaction clips, GUIA uditor achieves a 95.23% Macro-F1 Score in logging significant events and, crucially, its two-stage forensic query engine successfully retrieves the correct evidence as the top result for over 90.20% of natural language questions. An end-to-end evaluation on three modern smartphones shows that the full pipeline, including on-device MLLM inference, adds 2.1W of power draw and 7.4s of per-event latency, with a peak memory footprint of ~3.1GB. These results show that post-hoc GUI forensics can run on modern mobile devices and provide useful context for guardian-led safety review.

As artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) become embedded in research and publishing workflows, the scholarly community faces growing pressure to ensure their responsible and transparent use. The L-O‑C‑A‑D (Limitations, Ownership, Confidentiality, Accuracy, and Disclosure) Checklist, developed at EDP Sciences, offers authors, reviewers, and editors a practical, evidence‑based framework to assess and document their use of AI tools throughout the research and publication process. The checklist builds on the conceptual model proposed by Dr. Zhou in his Scholarly Kitchen article on the risks, rewards, and responsibilities of AI in peer review, broadening it into an operational, user-friendly tool suitable for diverse research contexts. The L-O‑C‑A‑D Checklist integrates guidance from the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), the European Association of Science Editors (EASE), and the STM Integrity Hub to create a consolidated, practice‑oriented resource. The L-O‑C‑A‑D Checklist helps users identify and mitigate key risks associated with AI systems, including training‑data opacity, model drift, hallucinations, privacy vulnerabilities, copyright ambiguities, and accountability challenges. It prompts users to assess data quality, avoid sharing confidential or unpublished material, verifying model versions, and ensure meaningful mandatory human oversight. It provides structured guidance for transparent AI disclosure. By promoting transparency, reproducibility, and human accountability, the L‑O‑C‑A‑D Checklist supports the principles of Open Science and strengthens integrity within AI‑augmented scholarly communication. This poster introduces the checklist, its rationale, and its practical applications for responsible innovation across the research ecosystem. This checklist is intended as a practical resource for the scholarly community and to evolve through collaborative feedback. Comments and suggestions are welcome at selina.labarbera@edpsciences.org

documents.abstract: The proliferation of consumer surveillance technologies and hyperlocal social media platforms reflects a broad sociotechnical shift in the ways ordinary citizens maintain community safety through their participatory surveillance. Recent qualitative research suggests that platform-based surveillance amplifies perceived neighborhood threat as residents adopt these tools to maintain urban order. How are these digital tools proliferating so rapidly despite historic declines in crime? To address this question, this article investigates the spatiotemporal diffusion of participatory surveillance across urban neighborhoods using dynamic spatial Durbin models with neighborhood and temporal fixed effects. The results show that participatory surveillance spreads through a self-reinforcing feedback loop in which surveillance activity clusters over time and propagates outward from early hotspots. These spatiotemporal patterns are consistent with a conceptual framework in which digital technologies localize a risk society by anchoring a diffuse sense of insecurity onto local spaces and legitimizing further informal social control. These findings have implications for understanding how surveillance technologies reshape perceptions of neighborhood disorder and reproduce urban inequality.

Survey research has taken up artificial intelligence quickly, largely because of speed, scale, and lower cost. Those same gains bring methodological risks that become especially serious where data are thin, several languages are in use, or cultural meaning is tightly layered. This article puts forward H-VALIDA (Hybrid Validation and Auditing for Localized, Interpretable, Documented, and Accountable AI-Assisted Surveys) as both a conceptual and an operational framework for AI-assisted surveys that are more reliable, more sensitive to context, and more firmly grounded in ethics. The framework draws together critical data studies, human-centred AI, the total survey error tradition, classical survey methodology, and decolonial principles of data governance. Seven interlocking pillars organise the work: Hybrid Human-AI Collaboration, Contextual Sampling, Algorithmic Auditing, Human Validation, Source Triangulation, Open Documentation, and Ethical Accountability. Those pillars are mapped onto an expanded total survey error taxonomy, and the CARE Principles for Indigenous data governance run through the design as a whole. The article is a methodological design study rather than a field experiment. Development of the framework followed a five-stage protocol: a diagnostic review of documented weaknesses in AI-assisted surveys; a structured synthesis of the literature; integration of principles; construction of the pillars; and operationalisation. Prospective appraisal rested on a specified heuristic rubric, a worked multilingual scenario, and a comparison with a purely automated baseline. No expert-panel scores, statistical tests, or national field implementation are reported here. Claims of improvement are therefore stated as theoretically grounded and operationally specified propositions that still require empirical confirmation. The central argument is that AI systems function as sociotechnical arrangements rather than as neutral instruments, and that validity depends on continuous human oversight, an open record of process, and deliberate adjustment to local conditions.

documents.abstract: How can artificial intelligence (AI) best support human problem-solving, creativity, and group work? I introduce a psychological account of narrative agency that formalizes how human groups learn from, communicate, and influence narratives in digital contexts. I then discuss how AI models impact human performance through a narrative agency lens, from authoring better essays to finding consensus online. Crucially, AI outputs are routed through a human's narrative agency to generate a result that causes change in the world. Designing human–AI systems around maintaining people's narrative agency is therefore essential for human–AI alignment.

Performance expectancy, individuals’ beliefs about the usefulness of digital transformation, could impact individuals’ intention, use, and satisfaction with technologies, yet remains an understudied topic among immigrant populations. Drawing on social capital theory, we examine how bonding and bridging social capital shape performance expectancy across different domains of digital transformation and whether these associations differ by nativity status. Using the 2022 Digital Divide Survey (N = 8,400; 7,000 native South Koreans, 700 marriage immigrants, 700 North Korean migrants), regression analyses showed that bridging social capital had positive associations with performance expectancy (b ranging from 0.43 to 0.62, p < 0.001), whereas bonding social capital was negative, particularly for networking (b = −0.09, p < 0.001) and remote work/learning (b = −0.08, p < 0.001). North Korean migrants reported the highest adjusted means of performance expectancy across all domains. Results highlight that diverse social networks generate greater perceived benefits from digital transformation.

Automated decision aids may undergo silent reliability degradation, in which performance declines without explicit warnings, confidence cues, or reliability-state feedback. In such situations, humans must infer whether automation has degraded from sequences of correct and incorrect outputs. This study examined the computational mechanisms underlying first failure reports in an industrial visual inspection task. We conceptualized silent-failure perception as a training-baseline-referenced first-report problem and compared five candidate mechanisms within a shared discrete-time hazard framework: Bayesian reliability learning, Delta-rule learning, CUSUM cumulative-deviation inference, recent-window heuristic monitoring, and a no-learning/reporting-tendency baseline. Trial-level data from 60 participants were analyzed across three levels of failure severity and two levels of initial reliability, yielding 720 participant-scenario observations with first-report times or right-censored outcomes. Participant-grouped 10-fold cross-validation showed that the Delta-rule learning model received the strongest predictive support among the five candidate mechanisms for participants whose data were entirely excluded from model estimation. This model-relative result is consistent with a baseline-referenced current-state tracking account: trial-level outcomes recursively update an estimate of the automation's current error state, and first-report probability increases when that estimate shows sufficient deviation from the training baseline. Failure severity primarily shaped the density and persistence of degradation evidence, whereas initial reliability shaped the experiential baseline against which later errors were interpreted. These findings provide a mechanistic account of silent-failure perception and inform the design of reliability-transparent automated systems.

Introduction Virtual technology offers a promising tool for encouraging engagement in exercise, as it can provide the user with enhanced visual stimuli and accessible metrics; however, the specific features within that technology that contribute to motivation and participation require further investigation. This study examined how different visual displays and the presence of a second rider influenced motivation to exercise using virtual technology. Methods Twenty-four young adults completed a 3-km cycling course on the same virtual track under three counterbalanced conditions including (a) a metrics-only ride, where a screen in front of the rider displayed only standard performance variables (e.g., power, cadence), (b) a solo-virtual ride, which was identical to the previous condition, but with the addition of the participant being depicted on the screen as an avatar amongst virtual scenery, and (c) a paired-virtual ride, that contained the same elements as the previous two conditions, but with the addition of a second rider represented on the screen as an avatar. Results The quantitative results, which included performance-related variables (cadence, power, speed, and heart rate), measures of intrinsic motivation, and ratings of perceived exertion, revealed significantly higher values for the paired-virtual condition compared to both the metrics-only and the solo-virtual conditions. Differences between the metrics-only and the solo-virtual conditions were isolated to interest-enjoyment and effort-importance. Brief interviews with participants indicated that the paired-virtual condition produced heightened levels of enjoyment and competitive drive which motivated participants to exert more effort. The solo-virtual condition was reported to be relaxing, but it was also reported as the least engaging. The metrics-only condition provoked negative emotions due to the absence of distractions and a heightened focus on internal cues. Discussion The results highlight the psychological mechanisms that influence motivation and engagement when using virtual exercise technology.

Recent autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) agents have made significant progress on public leaderboards. Often motivated by progress stagnation over long-horizon cycles and limited Large Language Model (LLM) primitives, modern MLE agents are deployed on top of increasingly elaborate machinery: multi-agent orchestrators, dedicated retrieval subagents, and more. While such harnesses expand, the use of more primitive but improved coding agents - where LLMs have direct access to the execution environment through read, write, and bash primitives - has received little attention in the field. In this paper we find that, under an equal time budget and the same frontier LLM backbone, open-source state-of-the-art harnesses provide no advantages over a single session of a minimal-harness coding agent baseline, pointing to the backbone as the primary driver for performance. Via a series of large-scale systematic ablation studies, we argue that the machinery layers become redundant in the coding agent setting. We conclude that the effort spent elaborating hand-crafted harnesses around strong models yields poor returns for current MLE benchmarks.
